newsitem.title: UK: British jobless data exaggerate labour mkt health.
newsitem.headline: British jobless data exaggerate labour mkt health.

text.p: British monthly unemployment data, due out at 0830 GMT Wednesday, will almost certainly show another impressive fall in March.
But extensive changes to the way government officials measure the jobless total mean the figures hugely exaggerate the health of the labour market, analysts say.

The picture painted by the official monthly figures is a rosy one. Unemployment has fallen for 16 months in succession and hit a six year low in February. The unemployment rate is fast approaching 6.0 percent, unrivalled by Europe's major economies, and the jobless total has fallen by a third since 1992.
But scratch the surface and cracks soon start to appear.

Five years of economic growth has yielded only a tiny increase in employment. Job creation is patchy, has fallen far short of expectations, and is growing well below the rate the huge monthly falls in unemployment suggest.
A recent report by investment banking group HSBC said the unemployment rate could be as high as 14 percent if measured in the same way as other European economies.

And the independent Employment Policy Unit said on Tuesday that at the end of 1996 18.7 percent of households had no-one in work, a sharp contrast to the official unemployment rate in December of 6.7 percent.
Many economists say the big unemployment falls seen in the last six months have had more to do with changes in the way the figures are calculated in Britain than economic growth.

Since the Conservatives took office in 1979 they have changed the basis of calculating the total over 30 times and Britain uniquely measures unemployment as people eligible for benefit and able to prove they are actively seeking work.
The most recent change came in October when the government scrapped unemployment benefit and replaced it with the jobs seekers' allowance which brought with it more rigorous eligibility criteria.
Unemployment falls accelerated from an average of 25,000 per month to 70,000 per month as administrators struggled with a backlog of claims.
Now even the government, usually keen to trumpet any economic success before the May 1 election, has been embarrassed into admitting the data exaggerate its employment record.
On the second day of the election campaign, the usually irrespressible Deputy Prime Minister Michael Heseltine confessed that only about half of the monthly falls were due to job creation.
"Something like half the reduction that we're seeing is through new jobs," he said after official figures showed a massive 68,200 fall in February.

Statisticians have lost patience with the low quality of the British data, especially since plans to produce monthly data using internationally recognised methodology were shelved last year due to funding contraints.

"The claimant count is not trusted, is not based on any agreed concept of unemployment, is inconsistent over time due to changes in claimant system and cannot be used for international comparisons," the Royal Statistical Society said.
And many City economists say the monthly figures are useless.

"The monthly figures tell us nothing about the labour market. You really have to ignore it and concentrate on the quarterly Labour Force Survey(LFS)," said Simon Briscoe, UK economist at Nikko Europe.
LFS data, which uses internationally approved methodology, paints a bright but unremarkable picture about the British jobs market.
In the three months to November, when claimant unemployment fell by 114,000, unemployment as recognised by the LFS fell by just 32,000.
More importantly, it showed the record on job creation is far from distinguished.

Since 1992, employment has grown by just 388,000 in a workforce of around 25 million. This is in sharp contract to the monthly official figures which show unemployment down by 771,400 to stand at 1,815,300 in January.
"It's a fairly pathetic growth rate, especially when compared with the 1980s," said Briscoe.
"Longer term data show hefty jobs growth during the 1980s. That fell off dramatically during the recession and only about half the jobs lost then have been replaced in the present upturn.".
The bunching of new jobs in a handful of sectors and the quality of the new jobs created has also given the opposition Labour ammunition to attack the government's handling of the economy.
New jobs have been heavily concentrated in banking, finance and insurance, public administration education and health with swathes of the economy missing out altogether.
And in the last year, part time jobs have grown by 2.3 percent while full time employment by just 0.7 percent.
Opposition Labour says the economy has now million fewer permanant jobs and one million fewer full-time jobs than five years ago.
"Job insecurity is stalking the workplace, trapping millions of people in short term, casual and temporary jobs," said Peter Hain, an opposition employment spokesman.
But the government has defended its record saying the flourishing part-time and temporary sectors are a response to growing demand for this type of work.
Economists say this is partly true.

"Women have become a much bigger feature in the workforce and part-time work is popular among women," said Ian Stewart, UK economist at Merrill Lynch. "Job creation has to an extent been in tune with changes in the workforce."
And while research showed that for many others, part-time or temporary work was involuntary, it is often a useful foothold into the jobs market.
"This group often quickly moves into better paid parts of the workforce. Part-time work is a starting point and this group very fluid."
